An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and implies an integrated luminosity of 17 pb$^{-1}$. The triangular relationship between signal yield, time information, and anomalous coupling has been studied in detail, although certain groups have proposed alternative explanations for the shape of the fit residual vs. proper time plots that do not align with the behavior expected from a narrow resonance that decays via both strong and electromagnetic forces.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs and the search for regular solutions. Numerical methods tested include finite difference, spectral and local discontinuous Galerkin methods, with error analysis conducted for smooth cases and simulation results obtained for the rough case.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that they provide unique insights, these results highlight the importance of low-momentum correlations in offering precise constraints on theoretical models and enhancing our understanding of the collisions' initial conditions through quark--gluon scalar product correlations.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, we examine the feasibility of this approach and develop an algorithm to apply it, demonstrating its validity with respect to two data quality metrics: table completeness and the preservation of rows that meet certain dependencies. Also, we investigate a related algorithmic problem with differing objectives, specifically distinguishing between data entriesStatus(es) \{true, false, inconsistent\}. A comparison is made between our proposed framework and other approaches, and the underlying assumptions and design choices of our work are discussed. Finally, we outline potential research directions for future exploration.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we analyze the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating that its parameters can be efficiently estimated using the maximum likelihood method, and we propose an iterative generalised least squares forecasting procedure to generate accurate predictions. To demonstrate the practical application and performance of the TV-PARX model, we conducted simulation studies and real data applications, including comparisons with alternative models and predictions.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models.

While using photometry from stars to measure aerosol depth in the atmosphere is a simple concept, its usefulness for reaching high precision is limited. A major factor contributing to this limitation is the need for long observation periods, which makes achieving short-period measurements necessary for certain applications, such as monitoring stratospheric aerosols from volcanic eruptions, increasingly unfeasible. In this paper, we present an innovation that allows for the development of a photometric system with short observation periods by analyzing one side of a symmetric dual laser system installed on a single beam path. This innovation is demonstrated using measurements of vertical aerosol optical depth taken from the Pico das Tolas volcano in Ecuador Volcano, which exhibits asymmetric aerosol emission from its volcano, by analyzing one side of the symmetry and applying a photometric system from the volcano's emission. In this process, we are able to reach a random measurement precision of 0.001 over short periods, which is comparable to other systems that have reached similar levels of precision.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using convolutional neural networks has become popular. Existing methods are either based on training synthetic data or object parts segmentation. This paper presents a straightforward approach using real data that doesn't rely on these assumptions. The proposed method uses a two-step regression framework to reduce complexity and improve performance. The input is the difference map between the detected object and background, which is created using instance segmentation. We then detect the object's boundary and extract features from the difference map. These features help classify whether the object pose can be accurately regressed. If possible, a pose is regressed using a lightweight network with two branches: one for orientation and one for position. Otherwise, the instance is re-detected with a pose prior. We conducted experiments on three convolutional neural network architectures and two instance detection methods. The results show significant performance gains over the current state-of-the-art methods in the field.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972).
The Graphical Lasso framework encompasses both the Independent Components Analysis (ICA)
and the Graphical Gaussian Models (GGM) as subproblems, as demonstrated by Banerjee et al. (2008).
Our implementation leverages the original Python implementation by Dahl (2010) and
utilizes the CVXPY package for efficient solution. The GGLasso package features
multiple objective functions, including those for ICA and GGM, as well as
constraints such as positive definiteness, diagonality, and element-wise bounds,
and supports both coordinate descent and proximal gradient methods for scalable
solutions to large datasets, as well as Bayesian formulations with automatic
hyperparameter tuning.

Numerous numerical methods for solving partial differential equations have been developed, yielding accurate results for determining rigid-body properties of complex systems, such as proteins and DNA. However, these methods often yield inaccurate estimates of rotational and vibrational averaging in biomolecular configurations. A new class of numerical methods is presented that yields seamless, analytically derived thermal-averaging factors for biomolecular configurations, enabling the application to large, macromolecular systems with numerous rotatable bonds and vibrant modes, such as protein ligand complexes. This approach utilizes numerous standard numerical methods, including numerical integration over rotational and vibrational configurations, yielding direct, rotational-vibrational thermal-averaging factors for differential equations' solutions. Solutions to these equations yield rigorous, thermodynamic-free properties of biomolecular configurations, such as ground-state wavefunctions, yielding rotational-vibrational thermal-averaging factors from numerical methods, such as numerical grid methods, which can be determined from the numerous rotational and vibrational configurations of biomolecular systems. This approach yields rigorous, deuterated liquid-phase IUPAC standard gas-phase partial pressures for biomolecular ions, yielding precise, biomolecular ion masses and spectra's accurate interpretation.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes or when a complete cavity is created have been widely used but lack underlying theoretical explanations. To better understand these phenomena, we used high-speed photography to analyze spherical impacts and found that key speeds, previously thought to apply only to specific sizes, actually hold true for spheres of various sizes. Furthermore, we found two critical speeds, marking the beginning and end of the surface seal regime, are supported by theoretical calculations of the forces at play. This, in turn, shows that the forces influencing the closure of the cavity during the surface seal regime are global in nature, contrary to previous beliefs.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths. As a consequence, when we try to preserve these $\theta$-terms, we must include Witten's expected charged density monopole currents. However, when we try to diagonalize the kinetic matrix of the two-form fields, we must perform a change of basis in the vector of dual scalar fields, which in turn affects the heavy string modes and generates matter fields with an anomalous charge. An anomalous charge leads to the violation of any put upon universal symmetries. It is worth noting that this mechanism is inherent to any closed string theory and not unique to Type IIB.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable properties despite previous limitations in demonstrating both bright and silent exciton states, as well as coherent silent-phonon dynamics. By designing and manufacturing a semiconductor microcavity containing a quantum acoustic cavity and a dark exciton quantum dot, researchers have been able to drive the system into a strong coupling regime and observe the formation of a polariton mode through both theoretical and experimental analyses, all without relying on silent phonons. The desired condition required to achieve this strong interaction between the quantum components was achieved by adjusting the frequency of the laser to match that of a sideband, resulting in Rabi oscillations of silent-phonon numbers in the dark biexciton state for the first time in history. This breakthrough demonstrates the potential for engineering multi-phonon systems and could lead to breakthrough applications in quantum technology by harnessing silent excitons, phonons, and biexcitons as a versatile resource.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying different onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built. This framework employs artificial neural networks to predict specific properties of molecules and employs mixed integer linear programming to choose the optimal molecule from a vast combinatorial set. We have developed a solution algorithm based on the principles of policy optimization. Our method has been tested on various molecule design problems, demonstrating its capability to successfully design molecules with specified properties, including complex cases such as specifying multiple substituent positions on a benzene ring. Our framework has also shown the ability to incorporate prior knowledge into the design process and to ensure that designed molecules are synthetically feasible. Generated designs have been found to be chemically valid and feasible, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very challenging for manual outlining due to the esophagus's complex anatomical position, variations in patient posture, and low contrast with surrounding tissue. These issues are even more pronounced with external tumors that cause distortions and mass effects, which are often poorly defined in treatment planning CT scans. To address this difficulty, our study evaluates the efficacy of segmenting such targets using automated methods by training on various types of contrast-enhanced CT scans and ultrasound images, as well as scans without contrast administration. Our results show that including images from different contrast presentations helps animals with a specific condition called megaloblastic anemia, but using automated deep learning methods, we found that contrast enhancement does not significantly improve the accuracy of segmenting the target and target + dissection regions in CT scans. To assess the importance of different image features, we employed a technique called occlusion, combined with heat maps to visualize how features contribute to deep learning models. Our findings indicate that ultrasound images and non-contrast scans contribute little to improving the identification of tumors in the esophagus, and we observed that trained models often confuse tumors with physiological structures like gastric air when creating heat maps. Furthermore, our study reveals that deep learning models fail to detect telling features such as displacement of surrounding structures caused by the tumors. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling this problem, with a focus on evaluating and training deep learning models, providing a framework for future work using a classification problem to guide text summarization and translation. Furthermore, it outlines potential improvements for the model by incorporating contextual factors and linguistic knowledge.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives.

Tantalum oxide compounds have attracted interest recently, especially with developments in hyperloop technology, thanks to their high electron density. Another potential application arises from the unique properties of Ta and its oxides with a high atomic number. Here, we investigate the absorption and scattering of linear and circular H+ ions at 10 MeV with a new data set, which fills a significant gap in existing research that lacks experimental results for Ta with proton linear absorption data near this energy level and scattering results for Ta with higher energies. The combined cross-sections for circular and linear cross-sections were found to be nearly the same at 10 MeV, and the new data may have valuable applications in various fields, including hadrontherapy for cancer treatment and range shifters made from tantalum.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the hypothesis that circulation of accurate and misleading news is related to population density through online advertising trends, and we analyzed how this relationship varies based on regional characteristics, including the 2016 U.S. presidential election results, political news consumption, and personality traits like news circulation's connection to conscientiousness. We found that regions with lower population density disseminates misinformation more readily, and this trend is especially pronounced among Republicans, in election-marginal states, and in states with lower scores on the2016 U.S. presidential election results, states with lower scores on the personality trait of conscientiousness, and states with lower scores on the news consumption of the Washington Post. Our1: findings suggest that1: the drivers of online misinformation dissemination are deeply connected to broader sociodemographic and political patterns.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models. A suitable framework for this challenge is provided by the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically those based on the Weyl-Moyal M5-brane model with an extremely high symmetry of conformal, M\"obius and internal. In these highly symmetric theories, we can express the growth of state operator complexity in a basis of high-symmetry bases, using a parameter that represents symmetry breaking, as both state and operator complexity exhibits both expected universal features and distinctive growth patterns. Numerical findings also allow us to establish the validity range of Fuzzy Sphere approximations for field theory complexity.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant interest for addressing the pervasive missing data problem. Single-target recommendations often yield incomplete profiles, whereas leveraging underrepresented data across multiple domains can substantially enhance recommendation precision. Nevertheless, existing work primarily concentrates on the bi-domain scenario and overlooks multi-domain scenarios in addition to the varied scale of missing data in each domain. We introduce a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative (MSDCR) model that seamlessly addresses the varied sparse domains' collaborative challenge. In line with the bi-domain case, we employ an innovative cross-domain attention mechanism to establish a sophisticated relationship between user preferences in different domains for cross-learning. To effectively address the various missing data scenarios, we employ a domain adaptation mechanism that dynamically adjusts user embeddings for bi-domain and multi-domain scenarios respectively. We designed a back propagation mechanism that allows user ratings in each domain to contribute to the overall optimization objective, thereby facilitating effective knowledge transfer across the domains. Experimental validation across 5 datasets underscores the superiority of our MSDCR model over the state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation methods.

Convex optimization issues often take shape as disciplined convex programming problems, which can be resolved efficiently by solvers capable of recognizing and handling various types of convex constraints, including conic constraints. Although this category encompasses widely used constraints such as semidefinite ones, it fails to account for many conic possibilities that could potentially be leveraged to streamline specific problems. We introduce a novel set of conic constructs termed exotic cones, which are not natively supported by standard optimization tools but can be defined using simple mathematical relations that guarantee their cone properties. These cones can be seamlessly incorporated into DCP problems, and their implementation involves formulating their slice projections as semidefinite issues. As an illustrative example, we demonstrate how to construct a set of exotic cones tied to nonincreasing functions with nonnegative derivatives, and whose semidefinite formulations are derived from the work of Marshall and Olver.

The escalating volume of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis. Several methods have been explored, mainly by training models on manually checked data, though this approach is inefficient and may not scale well. A novel strategy was developed to develop and train an initial version without labeled data, subsequently using a small set of manually checked data to refine the model. This strategy leverages active learning to efficiently allocate the limited manually checked data, allowing for identification of difficult or unreliable model predictions and their correction. The results indicate that this method significantly enhances performance compared to various alternatives, making it a promising technique for future development of robust and scalable quality control systems.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. Within the bilepton model, heavy vector particles with defined quantum numbers should decay mainly into combinations of the third and second fermion families. Consequently, this implies that leptoquarks should decay predominantly into top+W or top+Z combinations, which should be observable at a top factory like the Super $t\bar{t}$ Collider (STTC).

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Zauzmer recently demonstrated that the base length using ordered generating sequences equals 2, building on the work of Coxeter and Peterson who initially explored this problem. Our research extends Zauzmer's results by proving the base length for the extended symmetric group Ans is also equal to 2. Additionally, computed base lengths for other group types, including alternating groups An, glider groups Sn+1, and their rotated versions An+1, are presented.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for the distance modulus that incorporates the effects of lensing and is consistent with general relativistic principles: $\mu^* = \mu - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\rm SNI}} w_i (s_i - \bar{s})^2$, where $s_i$ represents the individual SN Ia light-curve shape

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted without considering their crystallographic environment, our study provides precise measurements of the 0-0 and 1.1 eV peak positions and their temperature dependencies for T centers in both <100> and <111> silicon orientations. Our findings reveal that the temperature behavior of peak positions and their relative strengths remain consistent across these different crystallographic orientations above 20 K. Furthermore, this characteristic allows us to propose a simple model for damage centers, in which the formation process does not involve a substantial energy barrier related to crystallographic orientation, thus facilitating their creation through standard ion implantation techniques. Additionally, we observe extremely spin-orbit protected spin states with spin and nuclear spin interfaces, resulting in exceptionally long spin lifetimes that exceed 1 second at temperatures above 30 K, and we discuss the implications of these results for developing robust photon-spin interfaces for building silicon-based quantum networks.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input image, another that uses
partial context by isolating the image and some contextual features, and one
that uses full context without isolating the image, only the context and hidden
representations.
Initially, we analyze the effect of these different setup on the context usage
by Part A of the visual question answering (VQA) dataset.
This effect is studied in relation to different components available for the model,
such as the image, visible context, unknown context, and the hidden representation.
The model in each experiment is the same, and it is trained with different
combinations of these components as inputs.
The effect of the setup on the context usage is studied by identifying the
unknown, high effect region, where the model's performance notably drops due to
the absence of a specific component.
This effect is seen in relation to the detector's level of complexity.
Furthermore, we introduce the first study that examines the effect of these
different setups on the attention map, which reveals that the absence of the
image, only the context and hidden representation as inputs causes the model to
attend to the unknown region.
This effect is found to be more pronounced in high performance regions

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions.

We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube, under the assumption of a positive association. Specifically, under the Strong Rayleigh condition, we delve into inequalities proposed by Chatterjee, and develop a series of inequalities that extend the original framework. Furthermore, we investigate concentration inequalities for functionals of random vectors that experience benign symmetry, and we establish that this scenario also ensures the desired concentration behavior. We then provide applications of our inequalities involving the Bernoulli-Laplace model, as well as card shuffling models, and we demonstrate that our inequalities yield novel outcomes even for the Bernoulli-Laplace model.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties of incompatible transplants, yet these methods are costly, time-consuming, and come with heightened risks of infection and rejection. From an operational perspective, desensitization methods require patients to receive high doses of blood products from the donor, which increases the risk of complications. A potential solution to this issue is found in plasma pheresis from the donor, which involves the removal of incompatible antibodies present in the patient's blood. Although this procedure has not been previously performed, it has the potential to achieve transplants with lower levels of donor-specific HLA mismatches and lower complement-dependent cytotoxicity levels. A team of researchers from Italy has set out to explore the feasibility and outcomes of plasma pheresis from the donor as a novel desensitization method for kidney transplants.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely adopted, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of its functionality. We demonstrate that for n-gram text inputs, certain features can be safely disregarded during the training process, thereby simplifying the model's assumptions to non-singular linear systems of equations. We also develop a formulation that is equivalent in functionality but offers an optimized computational approach with significantly reduced complexity. A computational algorithm is proposed to efficiently solve this formulation, yielding gains in speed of up to two orders of magnitude. A (unintended) benefit arises as a by-product of this research. A particular aspect of the embedding space is revealed, a part that is previously unknown, a structure that is both fascinating and practically significant.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior, which encompasses solutions like Correlated Equilibria (CE) and Nash Equilibria (NE), is a key goal. This work proves that the probability space of rationalizable outcomes lies between that of Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and CE, positioning CE at one extreme and CCE at the other. Our theory identifies the gap between CCE and CE as resulting from the potential for agents to correlate their randomized actions based on shared observations of action choices and history. Despite this limitation, an $O(n^n T)$ algorithm is proposed to learn CCE from an external regulator with access to multiple learners, in a settings where settings are either full or partial information, based on action rewards and losses provided by the setting. This includes exploration-free algorithms for both semi-bandit ($F=1$) and bandit ($F=n$) cases. Moreover, when the number of agents is constant and settings difficulty is defined by action set size, our findings are notable.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies.

To accelerate policy convergence in complex, dynamic systems with multiple concurrent inputs, reinforcement learning agents often operate in environments that release information step-by-step. Researchers have investigated multi-step reinforcement learning, but traditional policy acceleration techniques fail when transferring 'batch' data, as they assume independence from the surrounding environment. Conversely, classical experience replay assumes a single-system environment, which does not transfer effectively across distinct settings due to stored redundancy. These conflicting issues give rise to a novel single-step policy acceleration technique based on transferring reusable 'batch' data, renowned for its efficiency and effectiveness in dynamic systems. Furthermore, the proposed method outperforms current single-step policy acceleration techniques, as well as methodsthat incorporate use of stored data, especially in rapidly changing environments, as demonstrated by the artificial life game.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 200,000 written conversational dialogue transcripts, 
each dialogue maintained by five distinct agents. We then explore various 
aspects of the dataset, including the diverse branching paths in our short 
dialogues, the cross-talk that occurs among the virtual agents, and the 
difficulty rankers must navigate when attempting to anticipate multiple 
textual outcomes. Ultimately, we introduce an innovative ensemble model 
capable of anticipating all potential future dialogue paths by automatically 
generating a set of text sequences, each with an equal probability of 
occurrence.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically focused on scalar-tensor gravity models. This software is based on the existing solver GLAM and has been enhanced to simulate a range of vector and scalar fields associated with gravitational theories, featuring support for several simplified models such as $f(R)$ gravity, chameleon fields, and symmetron fields. Additionally, we have integrated a general time-dependent solver for the field equations. With these capabilities, N-body simulations incorporating a dark matter ensemble interacting with vector and scalar fields can be generated. We have specifically developed and implemented the perturbation theory-based method "TAM" and the exact field dynamics approach "EDM" to generate $N$-body simulations of $f(R)$ gravity, demonstrating the efficacy of EDM in modeling the non-linear regime with high precision. Moreover, we have replicated the results obtained in prior research utilizing the Miller code.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence, fueled by a Bunsen burner, to assess its contribution to instability sounds. Prior research has considered flame dynamics in response to acoustic waves but overlooked temperature fluctuations resulting from heat variations. To address this shortcoming, the study's approach incorporates flame noise and thermal feedback into its model and compares its predictions with experimental and previously established data. Through this method, the study derives analytical expressions that illustrate how flame temperature fluctuations interact with flow velocity and acoustic modes within a jet flame. Comparisons with measured data show that the study's model accurately predicts acoustic oscillations, including their amplitude and phase, as well as flame shape oscillations. Furthermore, the study's model predictions align with observed asymptotic behavior at high frequencies but also reveal a discrepancy at lower frequencies that may be attributed to nonlinear effects, axial conduction, or assumptions made in the study's model. Additionally, unlike previous models, the study's approach predicts significant higher-order mode excitations, which were successfully validated with measured data.

We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the impact when this interaction breaches the lepton number, which directly leads to a significant influence on the $0
u  eta  eta$ decay, even when the dark matter has a substantial mass compared to neutrinos. Since the ultralight dark matter can be characterized as a classical field, its influence appears as a coherent, Weber-like signal in the experimental data seeking to detect a WIMPless effect. If the required coupling strength to produce a visible signal is around $10^{-11} \, 	ext{GeV}^{-1}$, then for the best current limits on $0 \, 
u \,  eta \,  eta$ decay, the best constraints on this interaction are not as tight, providing a substantial boost in sensitivity to WIMPless scenarios from existing $\, 0 \, 
u \,  eta \,  eta$ decay searches.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to derive the field equations of nonlocal gravity in a way that matches its original formulation, and then to analyze the conditions under which it reduces to traditional gravity theory in both special and general relativity contexts. The nonlocal gravity theory theory can be viewed as a nonlocal variant of the Einstein - Hilbert action, leading to the conclusion that nonlocality is characterized by an history-dependent action component, which may or may not be related to torsion, depending on the nature of matter present.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits across various genomic features. Our results show that SNPs influencing traits often reside in accessible DNA regions, and some traits are linked to specific biological functions. Notably, traits associated with immune system-related SNPs include conditions such as anemia, psoriasis and type 1 diabetes. By integrating multiple annotation types, we found that SNPs associated with intussception are located in previously unexplored regions of the genome related to chromatin structure and gene expression. In addition, we discovered strong overlaps between expressed genes and SNPs associated with brain-related conditions in neuronal genes, and that SNPs in enhancer regions associated with these conditions are located further from transcription start sites than in other parts of the genome.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, not
all pertinent research can be covered within this report. It primarily examines
measurements focusing on collective behavior in small systems and new results on
strangeness enhancement observed in proton-proton interactions. It is essential to
note that many notable findings have been excluded from the discussion presented
here.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling spin and energy levels via the stimulation of vibrations using THz radiation.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between NLI settings and the semantic variety of model responses. It was discovered that the metric effectively differentiates between models with varying levels of response diversity. To further validate its effectiveness, this metric was integrated into a loss function for training models, resulting in a model capable of producing responses with increased semantic variety. Secondly, this paper is notable for being the inaugural application of NLI-based metrics to evaluate model response diversity in casual conversations. This research is forward-thinking and contributes to the development of more versatile and creative neural conversational agents.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay research is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection method efficiencies across 
different data sets.  This challenge can lead to an increased complexity in 
interpreting decay signals and may result in the inability to draw meaningful 
conclusions about coupling properties of hadrons.  This report presents several 
strategies for resolving this problem, including methods for resolving background 
differences and smoothing efficiency curves, enabling the resolution of various 
interferences and the extraction of meaningful likelihood values describing 
multivariate signals.  By implementing these strategies, researchers can 
accurately compare different data sets and determine coupling properties of 
hadrons through the formation of combined amplitude models.  Overall, this 
report provides the means for the interpretation of final state interactions in 
multibody decays.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple astrophysical phenomena, including relativistic radiation energy flows, optical emissions, and radio signal variations. The model initially considers the phases of fireballs, where the radius is much smaller or larger than the characteristic distance, and it derives key results, such as optical luminosity being proportional to time squared and the radius to the power of four in the initial phase, and it is also shown that radiation mass varies with the radius to the power of two in both small and large radius phases. The model's predictions align with theoretical expectations and can be utilized to test new physics, including possible axion production in blazars, including the observations of Tarcis-1 and Tarcis-2, by comparing and contrasting their findings with the model's estimates of cross-sections, optically thin thickness of the axion field, and its implications for the decay of radiation mass.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities provided by non-contact actuators to satisfy constraints that are otherwise challenging to achieve, such as reducing impact forces during the transition phases of the gait cycle.

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an previously unknown source of slowdown, which was found to be more significant than previously thought.  Compared to an existing technique, HyperDegrade causes 2x more instructions to execute during the target trace and reduces the statistical significance of measurements by 10%.  The effects of HyperDegrade were observed to have a wide range across CPU cores, which prevents averaging out its effects, making it a powerful tool for side-channel attacks.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It is established that any knot can be transformed into the trivial unknot through a series of unknotting operations. This research delves into the various types of operations and their respective efficiencies. Particularly, we examine the consequences of several recent operations and determine that five of them, when applied repeatedly, guarantee the transformation of any knot into the trivial unknot. A distinct characteristic of these operations is that they lower the genus, which is a specific parameter that is always non-negative, inherent to the knot in question. The unknotting operations are defined as follows: for each operation, we provide a diagrammatic explanation and are able to demonstrate that they all result in the reduction of a specific parameter, which is the genus, of the knot in question. It is also observed that the first operation was previously mistakenly characterized in the literature, and we correct this by providing the accurate definition.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) integrated over the Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant, a singular, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two after accounting for scalar multiplication factors. Similarities can be drawn with a part of Mortier's research. Nonetheless, in contrast to but also inspired by his result, we derive our cocycle, I(X), through the use of graph-based configuration space integrals rather than combinatorial approaches used by Mortier.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options.
