We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in a given correlation function are stress-energy tensors. Consequently, this connection yields a direct link between the Casimir currents构成 of an energy-conserving three-point interaction in CFT$_2$ and the geodesic Witten amplitude comprising an interaction at the boundary of the energy surface in the AdS$_2$ space. Moreover, the same representation can be applied to describe the four-point interaction when the primary fields are stress-energy tensors, which can be interpreted as a generalization of the CHM result \cite{Campbell:2018cqa} for this particular case. By isolating the singularity of the conformal block operator in CFT$_d$ along a specific line in complex plane, we discover that it matches the contribution from a spinning geodesic in the AdS$_d$ space.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 2 up to day 412 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations revealed that SN~2020jfo exhibited a narrow H-alpha line, indicating a progenitor mass within the range of 10-12 times the mass of the sun. Furthermore, by combining near-infrared photometry with spectral modeling, we found that SN~2020jfo was likely associated with a dense stellar wind and did not have a significant field star component. In-depth analysis of its plateau phase showed that SN~2020jfo's mass outflow rate changed significantly during its plateau period, and its estimated opacities were more transparent than other similar supernovae. Its absolute peak magnitude of around -17.2 made SN~2020jfo the second-faintest hydrogen-rich Type II supernova recorded to date.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time. When trained solely on dark matter particle masses at an initial snapshot, the network's predictions diverged significantly from halo masses at a later point in time, particularly in regions with low halo mass. However, including velocity information narrowed the discrepancy between predicted and actual halo masses, particularly in scenarios with smooth matter distribution. The inclusion of velocity fields led to the formation of halo mass with $10^9 h^{-1} M_{\odot}$ mass scale ten times more frequently than would have occurred without them. These effects are evident even in scenarios with notable dark matter matter distribution, implying that local halo mass predictions cannot be explained by solely fitting the halo-sphere model. This study's findings are relevant to the application of neural networks to predict halo collapse through the use of phase-space information.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined by its position rather than its intrinsic properties. This results in defining the state of each element by four parameters: rest-mass density, specific angular velocity, specific entropy, and the ratio of specific angular momentum to the square of the distance from the rotation axis. 

This method of locating fluid elements has two primary applications: simulating the evolution of rotating stars from a given equilibrium configuration and modeling the growth of disks around black holes from specific initial conditions. 

We have created two distinct numerical algorithms for implementing this approach: the first assumes known outer boundary conditions, while the second determines them numerically. Both algorithms have been successfully used to produce equilibrium configurations in the Bardeen-Okun formalism under slow, constant entropy rotation, yielding a novel equilibrium configuration for a rotating star in general relativity.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types show that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which include combinations of black holes, neutron stars, or singular neutron star mergers. Combining results from these detections, scientists are capable of studying the universal characteristics and unique properties of the gravitational source in detail, as well as conducting the first instance of multi-messenger astronomy with certain events. Furthermore, by studying the gravitational waves produced during these collisions, it is possible to determine the astrophysical processes and population aspects that give rise to the formation of compact binary systems, as well as evaluating the degree to which general relativity theory is supported. This review discusses the current understanding of binary merger events, by examining the underlying mechanisms that lead to their formation, the theoretical predictions concerning their frequency of occurrence, and the methods used to observe and analyze them. By focusing on the relationships between the parameters of binary mergers, the masses of the formed objects, and the characteristics of their event events, it is possible to gain a deeper understanding of these complex events.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19 urban mobility restrictions significantly reduced face-to-face interactions, potentially hindering innovation, social cohesion, and economic stability in the long term. To address this challenge, this paper presents an urban mobility resilience index that measures the likelihood of random encounters in city centers. A machine learning approach was used to analyze 139 days of Google Mobility Report data from 34 major cities globally. Results indicate that some urban settings recovered more quickly than others, with differences in recovery rates being most pronounced in cities with populations exceeding one million. Furthermore, certain factors such as a city's GDP per capita, education levels, and GDP elasticity in relation to mobility were found to be correlated with its ability to be resilient. This study contributes to the understanding of urban diversity's role in innovation and collaboration by providing insights into its necessity for overcoming physical encounters' limitations imposed by health crises.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in material falling directly onto the star. Rather, it either forms distinct objects or causes the inner disk to switch from stable to unstable states through changes in their structural properties. An unstable state gives rise to powerful bursts of growth that align with observations of high-mass young stellar objects. Notably, the characteristics of these bursts vary greatly and can be influenced by variables such as: "Whether the star is fed by one or more objects; The mass, mass distribution and impact speeds of approaching objects; The behavior of the inner disk before and after each object's arrival; Whether objects collide before being consumed by the star." Furthermore, the model predicts that the debris disk's far-infrared and submillimeter emissions can provide valuable information about the population of objects fueling stellar growth.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with non-zero flow velocity, constant surface tension, and a specified depth. Numerical methods were employed to solve the nonlinear equations governing these waves. Initial calculations focused on weakly nonlinear effects, followed by a comprehensive nonlinear study. Our results reveal that the characteristics of the flow, particularly its intensity and the surface tension, significantly determine the wave pattern. In a without surface tension, our findings indicate that more intense flows require larger nonlinear corrections and that the lack of tension combined with high-speed flow leads to singular solutions. On the other hand, with surface tension, our data show that increasing the flow speed allows for nonlinear corrections to grow, delaying the appearance of dry patches. Also, our studies show that increasing the flow speed causes the critical nonlinear threshold to decline, but that this effect is more pronounced in the absence of surface tension. Moreover, our findings indicate that increasing the shear flow strength allows for broader periodic solutions, specifically those with two-bump patterns, and that these patterns become dominant in the absence of surface tension. Moreover, our studies reveal that increasing the flow speed leads to longer wavelengths, before waves experience breakers, particularly in the absence of surface tension. In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing methods may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel approach has been developed to navigate complex indoor environments with a mobile robot using structured light sonar and LiDAR for both mapping and navigation purposes. By leveraging deep neural networks, the robot is capable of creating performance-simulation images and combining real image data with range maps to produce accurate navigation maps in real-time. Experiments conducted on real-world indoor environments with varying levels of complexity and mobility have shown the proposed system's capacity to produce quality synthetic images and navigate unknown environments successfully.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, we detail our approach to utilizing BERT to refine annotations for each interaction. Specifically, we present three strategies to incorporate BERT into the labeling process: first, filtering out interactions with inadequate or malformed data; second, refining the semantic labels of existing interactions; and third, correcting the transcription text of interactions. We compare these methods to conventional manual verification techniques across multiple annotated iterations. Our findings suggest that BERT is capable of effectively identifying interactions with annotation issues, rectifying mislabeled interactions, and enhancing the precision of behavior labels. Moreover, our study reveals that BERT excels at identifying certain interaction problems but is less effective at detecting others, underscoring the necessity for diverse human-annotated feedback to identify annotation inconsistencies. Ultimately, our research contributes to the dataset by expanding the annotated behavior data and by identifying interactions with incorrect labels or transcription text.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drift in state vectors by using closed-loop control systems. Yet, in dynamic and unknown environments, these methods produce inaccurate maps due to the persistent movement of state vectors. To address this limitation, researchers have developed reusable methods based on planning instead, such as active sensor pathways that plan trajectories for state vectors within a bounded region. This paper introduces a novel type of active sensor pathway planner that ensures robust mapping by planning trajectories that avoid minimum curvature radii, leveraging a laser scanner's radius of curvature feature. The proposed method generates paths in 2D environments, utilizing the SkipNet, a deep reinforcement learning policy network trained to predict robot paths, and ensures map driftlessness by planning paths that maintain a closed-loop control system. The paper presents the algorithm's details, as well as results from theoretical and practical experiments to validate the approach's effectiveness.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices has historically been constrained by programming complexity, but the emergence of GPU technology has started to transform this perception. However, performance gains come with their own set of limitations. Our research introduces Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), a novel concept that enables precise comparison between SIMD and mass parallelism. In this approach, simultaneous execution of identical code by individual threads is made possible through the utilization of data partitioning techniques. We have implemented and tested the SMMO concept on two different SIMD architectures, achieving substantial performance improvements of over 1.5 times and 2 times respectively. Our findings offer an 8% minimum correction to previously assumed peak efficiencies of over 0.99, highlighting the importance of considering this approach in future high-performance optimizations.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms on the surface of Pb(111) were conducted with varying coverage levels. The resulting spectra exhibit features corresponding to specific magnetic orbitals and reveal interesting interactions between adatoms, which can be modulated by an external electric field. This dynamic behavior reflects the complex relationship between the adatoms, the superconducting surface, and any resulting coverage-induced effects. The proposed model offers a valuable tool for exploring quantum information processing applications and magnetic seed growth procedures, and by controlling the adoral alignment, researchers can mediate exchange interactions between adatoms, laying the foundation for scalable exchange coupling among various spin-based architectures.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of transiting exoplanets in distant star systems. The system known as Proxima Centauri b, discovered before $TESS$ launch, presents a unique opportunity for study given its close proximity. Recent $TESS$ observations of this system revealed additional potential planets, including one with a short orbital period and another further out that could support life. In order to better understand these young worlds, researchers analyzed $TESS$ data along with existing information from Proxima and its star system. By examining the brightness changes caused by the planets moving across their stars, scientists determined key characteristics of these planets, such as their density and surface conditions. However, $TESS$ data's limited resolution and short observation period present challenges in identifying smaller transits of the outer planet and determining their ages. Despite these challenges, researchers were able to determine that these planets reside in a dynamic environment and are likely in the process of forming.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a slightly higher formation energy than their substitutional counterparts.  Moreover, optical absorption spectra calculated for these defects lie within the UV range and correspond to a wavelength of 4.5 eV (275nm).  Given that TiO2 possesses inherent wide-band-gap characteristics, these defects could contribute to its photocatalytic activity when exposed to ultraviolet light.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate that sending a proton at the front can be used to identify the energetic particles emitted during the LHC interactions, which helps in detecting the production of top-quark pairs. By identifying these particles, researchers can identify the energetic particles emitted during the LHC interactions, which helps in detecting the production of top-quark pairs. I also discuss the possibility of using this method in future LHC interactions to detect the weak force acting upon a top-quark. An analytical method is proposed in which the particles emitted at the front from both interaction points yield the parton distribution functions for valence gluons, which contributes to the production of top-quark pairs.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. When high-energy photons generated by the plasma response to an intense laser encounter the same intensity, they can lead to the generation of positrons through a process known as the Breit-Wheeler process. In order to better understand how a process involving two steps compares to positrons that originate from within a laser focus, calculations have been performed on the positron production mechanism in which an intense circularly polarized laser interacts with a thin, solid target. In these interactions, electron-positron pairs are generated from the target by the laser, and then the resulting virtual electron undergoes a second process with a high-energy photon, leading to the creation of a positron. Since the target is extremely thin, the virtual electron retains much of the laser's polarization, and thus, the resulting positrons are expected to have a high level of polarization. However, as the transverse momentum transferred from the target to the virtual electron is much larger than the typical polarization measurement, the polarization levels are not uniform, and in many cases, they are quite low. This research has primary implications for upcoming experiments involving intense lasers and targets, and also opens up opportunities for creating highly polarized positrons.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages on-chip temperature variation to accelerate training in neuromorphic spike-based learning. A key feature of the designed sensor is its ability to accurately capture local thermal variations, enabling dynamic task scheduling in a multi-processor system by relocating temperature-sensitive tasks to less stressed processors. The temperature sensor includes a fully-differential CMOS bandgap reference circuit, fully-differential operational amplifiers, and temperature sensing circuitry. At room temperature, the designed reference circuit achieves a temperature coefficient of $20.44$ ppm/$\celsius$ and quality factor of 1.028, while the temperature sensor demonstrates high sensitivity of 1.04$\pm 0.02$ mV/$\celsius$ and low noise level of 2.04$\pm 0.09$ mK/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$. The designed sensor circuitry covers an area of 0.48 mm$^2$ and operates with a power consumption of 1.2 mW at a 10 MHz clock frequency. This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids. Initially, I examine the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids, demonstrating its homological properties through specific examples. Then, I investigate Grothendieck's relative Riemann-Roch theorem for Lie groupoids and establish its coherence under perturbations, utilizing relative Chern forms for non-Abelian 2-cochains. I further explore connections between this construction and the relativization of Chern forms developed by Baez and Schreiber, establishing a key relationship with that framework.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed a simple automatic label-free method for the second task. Our approach for the label-free task won first place, and our solution for classifying the outlier class largely contributed to the rankings of 2nd and 4th place in tasks 1 and 2, respectively.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids and subject to rotation, is perturbed by a fluid flow, causing fluid exchange through the membrane. With the aim of determining the conditions for the emergence of fingering instability in a rotating Rayleigh-Roberts experiment, a non-linear model is proposed to describe the membrane's response to tension variations and rotational forces. The model is solved analytically in the absence of rotation and a non-linearity approach is applied to account for increased rotation speeds, yielding an explicit formula for the critical rotation speed at which fingering instability arises. By examining the influence of rotation speeds, tension, fluid density differences, and radius of curvature, we find that the membrane's curvature plays a significant role in determining the appearance of instability, particularly in scenarios with large radius of curvature and large density differences, where non-linearity effects become dominant.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH over CN ratio is higher for cyclopentadiene but significantly lower for benzene. The formation of the cyclical compounds in TMC-1 can be attributed to a reaction pathway based on neutral-neutral reactions, which also suggests benzene's expected abundance should be comparable to that of cyclopentadiene.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling networks to focus on relevant source sentence parts to produce target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences but also heavily on previously generated target words, with networks often forming biases that are reinforced repeatedly. To address this issue, we present a novel adaptive attention mechanism that dynamically adjusts attention distributions based on previous target words' importance, effectively addressing unnecessary repetitions by encouraging a more diverse set of attention patterns and target words. Our proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through multiple benchmark datasets, showing that it addresses the repetitive problem and provides a significant BLEU score improvement that outperforms existing control methods. Additionally, we conduct generated sentence analysis and visualizations to further illustrate the underlying mechanisms of our approach, revealing that it jettisons unnecessary repetitions and produces diverse, grammatically correct sentences with meaningful patterns of attention.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and a wide range of admissible ranges. This allows us to identify a narrow range of parameter space where the model exhibits desirable phenomenological behavior. This space is suitable for matching observational data. Finally, we present specific solutions for the model's dynamics, which can be matched to the $\Lambda$CDM model, a key component of the standard cosmological model. These solutions result in the Hubble parameter evolving in time in a manner that is consistent with current data, including the latest Planck data set. In particular, we find that the model can reproduce the observed value of the dark energy statefinder parameter $s$ and the spectral index for scalar perturbations. This support can be seen from the cross-correlation between the model's dark energy sector and the inflationary paradigm, both of which reside within the same theoretical framework. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay data from the Markushanski group at Novosibirsk and the BES collaboration at Beijing, which have yielded significant results and maintained their importance over time. These observations have the potential to reveal a specific MeV-scale dark matter candidate, capable of evading experimental limits set by J/ψ decay into invisible matter, direct detection studies, and the cosmic radiation spectrum from the J/NAF detector. Moreover, our analysis indicates that certain radiation signatures from the J/NAF detector can be attributed to the decay of bound charmed nuclei, formed during the coalescence of $J$ mesons and $\bar{\Lambda}$ baryons, along with a distinctive peak near 3.92 GeV in the radiation spectrum that may be due to these dark nuclei.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by its increment distribution $\law(S_1) \in \mathcal{M}(2,\sigma^2,\infty)$ and can be represented as $\law(-S_1) \in \Gamma(2,\sigma^2,\infty)$. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is defined by the relation $\left(\frac{\phi(x,b)}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1-x}{e^{b/x} - 1}$, where $b \geq 0$ is the maximal value of $x \in [0,1)$ for which $\phi(x,b) > 0$. This b is determined by the ratio of the right and left tails of the random walk's increments.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using nucleus segmentation, which has historically depended on hand-crafted methods. To enable fully automatic nucleus segmentation, deep learning, specifically neural networks, has been adopted, and recent advancements have seen remarkable progress. Nevertheless, training these models effectively remains a challenge due to the scarcity of well-annotated data. This paper presents an exploration and benchmarking research on training nucleus segmentation models, examining various approaches, data augmentation, and network architectures. Notably, it investigates difficult sample annotation problems and presents essential insights for training high-performance models. By leveraging extensive experiments across multiple datasets, including both in-domain and out-domain augmentations, and even training with synthetic data, the presented results demonstrate that by carefully addressing sample annotation issues and employing specific augmentation techniques, high-precision model performance can be achieved. Given its comprehensive examination and robust benchmark results, this research provides a thorough foundation for addressing the generalization problem in nucleus segmentation, as well as addressing specific issues such as limited data and class imbalance.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and a sufficiently large integer. Let G be either a group associated with a unitary group of rank 2n or an orthogonal group of rank 2n defined over this field. For any given irreducible representation that is both admissible and generic of G, we can find a unique automorphic representation of GL_n for which this representation is isomorphic to this irreducible representation restricted to it. This is true provided the representation is isomorphic when restricted to the residual characteristic.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted to match a modified gravitational theory with a non-minimal interaction between the curvature and a scalar field. The holonomic constraints imposed on parallel transport create two distinct scenarios: one where the geometric field satisfies the Weyl-symmetric condition and couples to the curvature in a specific way, and another where the nonlinear transport condition results in a decoupled, mass term for the geometric field. Establishing the theory's Hilbert action's equivalence to the modified gravitational theory's holonomy approach proves crucial in deriving the theory's field equations. The equation of motion for the holonomic variant allows us to discover a class of radial solutions with a constant holonomy, and we identify the corresponding general solution in a holonomic coordinate system. Notably, the theory's holonomic approach generates a non-linear, non-local mass term interaction that does not align with the standard non-minimal coupling between the curvature and the scalar field.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualization of tissue pathologies by detecting changes in tissue stiffness. Accurate estimation of displacement in various directions via 2D ultrasound beams is crucial for effective 2D elastography. In this study, we developed a novel approach called Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) imaging and applied it to construct high-quality delay-and-sum beamformed images for elastography in multiple directions by simulating a point receiver array. In VSSA, we tested different numbers of virtual sources to assess their impact on image quality. In contrast to traditional Synthetic Aperture (SA) imaging, VSSA provides lobes compression and enhanced contrast and elasticity estimation by simulating virtual sources. In comparison studies using both simulated and experimental data, VSSA showed superior performance over SA and matched the results obtained with a large aperture aperture and high sampling rate (HS-LAA) approach. In elastic and stiff region elasticity maps, VSSA images demonstrated elastic and stiff region visualization that were more accurate than SA images.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. By integrating over specified reaction channels, we determine the distribution functions for W and Z particles from muon colliders in a precise and unambiguous manner. Specifically, we calculate the leading order muon distribution functions for W and Z particles, denoted as $f(\mu,\xi)$, and subsequently, we evaluate the reaction cross-section for muon colliders, including a demonstration for the leading order process of muon fusion, including its radiation correction to the leading order in particle interactions (QCD and EW), and we compare the predicted reaction rates with existing studies.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance. To overcome this challenge, we propose learning separate dynamics
models for each task while encouraging their memory components to develop
synergistic representations through可分性约束 (divisibility constraints). Our
approach demonstrates a significant improvement over the baseline method that
employs a shared dynamics model in several multi-task reinforcement learning
scenarios.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others, by leveraging prior knowledge about high-quality images to recover them from incomplete observations. A significant challenge in this field is ensuring the generated solutions are diverse, reliable, and high in quality. In this work, we propose a new method that samples from the posterior distribution in a way that balances efficiency, diversity, and precision. Our approach, called Diversity and Accuracy Estimation using Importance (DAM-I), employs a pretrained generative model, such as a generative adversarial network, to generate potential solutions, which are then adjusted using an importance score derived from the data. By applying importance estimation techniques, we aim to create a set of optimized importances that help achieve this goal. We evaluate our method on image reconstruction from sub-Nyquist sampled Kt-lines in KTR and compressed sensing, and demonstrate its effectiveness through experimental results.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant manifolds associated with fixed points and periodic orbits, focusing on their definitions, key properties, and various applications. In addition, we present multiple examples illustrating the practical importance of invariant manifolds.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble.

This paper presents a new end-to-end statistical voice transformation method called Note-specific Transformer Voice Transformation (NTVT). Traditional dynamic speech transformation models using neural networks have achieved natural sound changes, excluding pitch-dependent effects. Our research fills this gap by developing a pitch-dependent neural network that incorporates convolutional network attention mechanisms and dilated components, creating the Note-dependent Dilated Convolution Neural Network (NDCNN). Building on the NDCNN framework, we introduce a generator based on the network, which is enhanced with an auxiliary waveform generator using a plectra model, resulting in a new voice transformation framework, NTVT. A primary target fundamental frequency guide is provided by an frequency following module, enabling the Voice Transformation Framework (VTT) to perform voice transformation without requiring a fundamental frequency discriminator, leading to a new voice transformation model (NTVT). Experimental findings indicate that our proposed method (NTVT) yields an overall mean PCM score of 10.5, an improved PCM score in the frequency range of 500Hz (10.0), and a fundamental frequency correlation of 0.99, demonstrating significant advancements over previous research.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory. Furthermore, this equivalence serves to validate claims of Morita invariance for various bicategories, including those arising from Quillen bicategories of derived categories, leading to proofs of previously incongruous homological identities.

Our primary goal is to pinpoint sound sources in videos without any labeling. Our starting point builds on the work in [1], which employed a technique called semantic self-supervised learning (SSSL). Initially, we incorporate hard sample mining into our HS2SSSL method, which enhances performance by focusing on difficult samples. Our model then undergoes further refinement using a cross-modal attention mechanism and a new temporal attention mechanism designed to accelerate training while enhancing efficiency. Experimental results show that our method achieves superior performance compared to the baseline, with improvements of 10 and 8 MACO in the CHiME4 dataset and 5 MACO in the KcSCLD4 dataset, respectively.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phase ordering in these materials, often ignoring the effects of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.
